attach.why: Supplies each candidate's production rank among peers as one ballot feature for nfl.vote_outcome_model; it is not the winner rule, because the AP winner is the highest total of ranked-ballot points, not the maximum of production.

Ranked-ballot aggregator (50 voters; MVP top-5 10-5-3-2-1 and, per the 2025 AP announcement, top-5 10-5-3-2-1 for all eight AP awards; earlier non-MVP schemes unverified) that turns candidate features into winner probabilities in stage s6.

unreg:team_and_event_counting_specials.target: A team's or both teams' additive count in a game (field goals, sacks, total yards, successful 2-point and 4th-down conversions) or a team's interception in a multi-game window, relative to a threshold.
unreg:team_and_event_counting_specials.mechanism: Per-game counts are opportunities times a per-opportunity rate: field goals follow drives that stall inside the kicker's range, sacks follow opposing dropbacks times a pressure-to-sack conversion, yards follow plays times yield per play, and two-point and fourth-down conversions follow each coach's decision to try times a success rate, all reshaped by score path, weather and overtime. Counts are overdispersed and discrete, so thresholds are tail masses of a mixture over score states; both-team counts add a script-driven negative dependence between teams. The next-interception window is a survival probability over several games compounding per-game hazards against specific opposing quarterbacks.

attach.why: Starting quarterback status and sack avoidance change dropbacks, sacks and interception hazards for team sacks, game sacks and the next-interception window.
In-game quarterback exit risk changes the opposing sack and interception pools and the team's yards; staged in the sack and interception stage.
Practice and designation vintages feed the starting-quarterback availability probability used by the sack count and the window interception hazard.
Coach aggression on fourth downs and two-point tries and tempo drive field-goal attempts and the conversion counts.
Go-for-it versus kick policy and two-point policy by state set attempts for field goals and for the 2-point and 4th-down conversion counts.
Go-for-it policy on 4th-and-goal decides two-point attempts and goal-line fourth-down tries counted by KXNFL4DCONV and KXNFL2PTCONV.
Opposing defence interception propensity adjusted for quarterback quality is the per-game factor in the next-interception window hazard.
Sampled rules text fixes the counted object, thresholds, first-score and penalty clauses and what is left unstated (overtime, postponement, source), so settlement is read from it and not assumed.
In-game injury exit risk of the starting quarterback changes comeback and lead-change odds from the exit onward, a path event that pregame ratings cannot see.
Quarterback-specific hazard of leaving before the end of the game, by lead size, clock and mobility, used to switch the trailing or leading team to a backup in the simulated path.
Overtime points increment and probability by rule era: the only attached input that models whether and how overtime changes scores, needed for the regulation-only versus full-game readings.
Probability that a game ends level after overtime, which decides whether a game that was tied late can still produce a comeback win or a lead change.
Drive-result probabilities by start position over all drives, supplying mid- and late-game drive rates that the first-four-drives input does not cover.
Opponent-adjusted per-drive TD and FG rates by period, so the generator uses period-specific scoring for the 10-12 drives of a game and not only early-game rates.
Sampled rules text fixes the counted object, thresholds, first-score and penalty clauses and what is left unstated (overtime, postponement, source), so settlement is read from it and not assumed.
End-of-half hurry-up and clock management, the situation in which a quarterback spike on or inside the 1 can occur, which is a clock decision and not a pass call.
Quarterback-specific hazard of leaving the game by lead size, clock and mobility; the exit event that can put a non-quarterback in as the emergency passer.
Probabilities that a team's QB1 and QB2 slots are filled by named players, which tells who the emergency passer would be and whether a backup is listed at another position.
